l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Egypt is presented as a land whose legislators established unusual and admirable laws. Egyptian priests claim that many Greek religious rites, laws, sciences, literary ideas, and artistic practices originated in Egypt.

l: Egyptian legislators, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: The Egyptian legislators are said to have created laws governing public life, religious worship, military discipline, royal administration, contracts, and provincial government. Their laws were highly praised, although many were later abrogated by the Macedonians.

l: Egyptian laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Written laws were first instituted in Egypt, according to the account, by Menes, who pretended to have received them from Mercury. The device of attributing laws to a god or divine being is said to have encouraged people to obey them.

l: Menes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Menes is described as a heroic and famous man who was the first in Egypt to institute written laws. He claimed that Mercury had given him the laws and that they would greatly benefit the public.

l: Lycurgus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Lycurgus is said to have used the same device as the Egyptian lawgivers by claiming that Apollo gave him his laws. He is also reported to have traveled to Egypt and borrowed some of the laws he established in Sparta.

l: Sasychis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Sasychis is described as the second Egyptian lawmaker, a wise and prudent prince who added laws concerning the honor and worship of the gods. He is also credited with discovering geometry and teaching astronomy.

l: Sesostris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Sesostris is identified as the third Egyptian lawmaker. In addition to his military achievements, he established laws for Egyptian military discipline and organized military affairs.

l: Bocchoris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Bocchoris is described as the fourth Egyptian lawmaker, a wise and prudent king who regulated royal matters and established rules for contracts. His judgments were considered so excellent that many were still remembered, although he was said to have been physically weak and extraordinarily covetous.

l: Amasis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Amasis made laws to direct the Nomarchi in their governments and brought the provinces of Egypt into order. He was regarded as wise, just, and good, and was elevated to the throne despite not being of royal blood; he also advised the Eleans and warned Polycrates against tyrannical rule.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Darius, the father of Xerxes, is called the sixth maker of laws for the government of Egypt. He rejected Cambyses' impiety, studied Egyptian theology and sacred records with the priests, imitated the ancient kings' kindness toward their subjects, and was honored by the Egyptians as a god during his lifetime.

l: Orpheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Orpheus is said by the Egyptian priests to have traveled to Egypt and brought Egyptian religious rites and ceremonies to Greece. They attribute to him the Greek accounts of the Orgia, the underworld, the punishment of the wicked, the Elysian fields, and Mercury's role as conductor of souls.

l: Daedalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Daedalus is said to have visited Egypt and imitated its labyrinth. The Egyptians also claim that he made the porch of Vulcan's temple at Memphis and that a wooden statue made by him was kept in a temple and honored as a god.

l: Homer, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Homer is said to have come to Egypt and to have drawn ideas for his poetry from Egyptian customs and stories. The account specifically connects his descriptions of the underworld, the movement of Jupiter and Juno into Ethiopia, and Helen's potion with Egyptian practices or traditions.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: The Nile is identified with the Oceanus mentioned in Homer's poetry because the Egyptians call the Nile by that name in their own language. Egyptian funerals described in the unit involve transporting the dead across the river.

l: Memphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, • And now it is necessary for us to speak of the legislators of Egypt^
s: Memphis is associated with the Egyptian funerary landscape near the lake called Acherusia, which is surrounded by ponds, meadows, woods, and groves. The city is also said to contain the stately porch of Vulcan attributed to Daedalus, and a nearby field called Golden Venus.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Book II begins its account of ancient Asia with Ninus, the first Assyrian king recorded in history. Ninus conquers Babylon, Armenia, Media, and many other Asian countries, builds Nineveh beside the Euphrates, and later invades Bactria. Semiramis, whose reported origins are connected with Derceto and pigeons, helps capture Bactria and becomes queen after her husband Menon dies and Ninus later dies. Ninus leaves Semiramis as regent for their son Ninyas.

l: Book II, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Book II describes events in ancient Asia, beginning with the Assyrian empire. Its first chapter concerns Ninus, Semiramis, Nineveh, Bactria, and the early Assyrian conquests.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Asia was formerly governed by native kings, though no history of their memorable actions or names was extant. Ninus sought to conquer all the region between the Tanais and the Nile, except the Indians and Bactrians at first.

l: Assyrian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: The Assyrian empire is introduced through the conquests of Ninus, its first king recorded in history. It expanded across many countries of Asia under his rule.

l: Ninus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Ninus was the first Assyrian king recorded in history and was warlike, ambitious, and successful in conquest. He subdued many countries, built Nineveh, captured Bactria, fathered Ninyas by Semiramis, and died leaving Semiramis as regent.

l: Assyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: The Assyrians served in Ninus's armies during his conquests. In the first battle against Bactria, the Bactrians defeated and pursued them, killing a hundred thousand, but the Assyrians later overcame the Bactrians by superior numbers.

l: Arabia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Arabia was described as inhabited by strong and freedom-loving people who resisted foreign rulers. Ninus allied with Arieus, king of Arabia, and later sent the Arabian king back with rich spoils and gifts.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: The Babylon that existed later had not yet been built when Ninus invaded the region. At that time the province of Babylon contained several considerable cities, whose inhabitants Ninus subdued and made tributary.

l: Nineveh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Nineveh was a great city built by Ninus near the Euphrates and named after him. It was inhabited chiefly by wealthy Assyrians, though people of other nations were also allowed to settle there.

l: Euphrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: The Euphrates ran near the city that Ninus built, Nineveh. The city's large earth mound over Ninus's burial place was visible from many furlongs away across the plain near the river.

l: Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Bactria was a strong country with many large and populous cities, including a principal city also called Bactria. Its king Oxyartes raised four hundred thousand men, but Ninus eventually subdued the province and took its wealth.

l: Semiramis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Semiramis was presented as a woman of exceptional beauty, intelligence, courage, and ability. She helped capture Bactria, became Ninus's wife and the mother of Ninyas, and ruled as queen regent after Ninus's death.

l: Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Syria contained Ascalon and the lake and temple associated with Derceto. Ninus also returned to Syria after his earlier campaigns and marked out the place for building Nineveh.

l: Menon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Menon was a high officer, president of the king's council, and chief governor of Syria. He married Semiramis, but hanged himself after Ninus demanded that he give her to the king.

l: Ninyas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Ninyas was the son of Ninus and Semiramis. After Ninus died, Semiramis retained the kingdom as regent for him.

l: Nineveh's construction, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Ninus built Nineveh near the Euphrates after his earlier conquests. The city had a long circuit of four hundred and fourscore furlongs, walls a hundred feet high, broad ramparts, and fifteen hundred high towers.

l: Ninus's conquest of Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Ninus conquered Babylon, Armenia, Media, Egypt, Phoenicia, Coelosyria, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Lycia, Caria, Phrygia, Mysia, Lydia, and many other countries. He subdued nearly all of Asia between the Tanais and the Nile within seventeen years, except the Indians and Bactrians.

l: Ninus's invasion of Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: After an earlier unsuccessful attempt, Ninus invaded Bactria with an army said by Ctesias to include seventeen hundred thousand foot, over two hundred and ten thousand horse, and ten thousand six hundred hooked chariots. He divided the army because of the narrow and difficult passages.

l: siege of Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Ninus's forces defeated the Bactrians in the open country and subdued their other forts and castles, but the city of Bactria resisted because of its strength and provisions. The siege continued until Semiramis identified a neglected route to the citadel.

l: capture of Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Semiramis led men over the rocks, crossed a deep trench, and seized part of Bactria's castle. After she signaled the attackers, the defenders panicked, abandoned the walls, and the city was taken.

l: Semiramis's accession, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Semiramis rose to royal power after Menon hanged himself when he refused to surrender her to Ninus. After Ninus died, she became queen regent and held the kingdom for their son Ninyas.

l: Ninus's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK IL
s: Ninus died after returning from Bactria and settling affairs throughout the province. Semiramis buried him in the royal palace beneath a huge mound of earth and then ruled as regent.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: Semiramis undertakes the construction and adornment of Babylon, assembling two million workers and completing its principal works with architects and artists. The city is built around the Euphrates and enclosed by a massive wall with turrets, while a bridge, embankments, palaces, a vaulted passage, and a temple are added. The unit also describes Babylon’s hanging garden, later attributed to Cyrus, and the commercial cities Semiramis established along the Euphrates and Tigris. Over time, the palaces and other structures decay, and much of Babylon becomes farmland and pasture.

l: Semiramis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: Semiramis, ambitious to surpass her predecessors, organizes the building of Babylon and gathers two million men from throughout her empire for the work. She oversees the city wall, bridge, embankments, palaces, vaulted passage, temple, and other works, and establishes additional cities and marts along the Euphrates and Tigris.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: Babylon is described as a great city through which the Euphrates runs, containing massive walls, palaces, a temple, a bridge, and a hanging garden nearby. Over time, its palaces and other structures are consumed or greatly damaged, leaving only a small part inhabited while much of the area within the walls is used for tillage and pasture.

l: city (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: The city is built in the province of Babylon with the Euphrates running through its middle. It is surrounded by a wall, includes a space between the wall and the houses, and is connected across the river by a bridge.

l: Euphrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: The Euphrates runs through the middle of Babylon, dividing the city into eastern and western sides. Semiramis builds a bridge over it and temporarily diverts its course while constructing a vaulted passage between the palaces; the river is then returned to its ancient channel.

l: city wall (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: The city wall is described as extending 360 furlongs in circuit, or 365 furlongs according to other writers, and as being made of brick cemented with brimstone. It has numerous stately turrets, great height and breadth, and a two-hundred-foot space separates it from the houses; morasses provide natural defenses in some places.

l: bridge (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: Semiramis builds a bridge across the narrowest part of the Euphrates, five furlongs long and thirty feet broad. Its stone pillars are joined with iron hooks and lead, protected by pointed defenses against the current, and floored with cedar, cypress, and palm timber.

l: palaces of Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: Semiramis builds two palaces at the ends of the bridge, one on the east side of the Euphrates and one on the west, with views over the city and access to its convenient places. The western palace has several enclosing walls decorated with representations of living creatures and hunting scenes, while the other has statues, armies, and hunting scenes; the palaces later decay or are greatly damaged.

l: hanging garden (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: The hanging garden near the citadel is said not to have been built by Semiramis but by a later prince called Cyrus for a Persian courtesan. It consists of ascending arches and planted terraces supported by strong masonry, with conduits and engines that draw water from the river to irrigate the garden.

l: building of Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis^ was naturally of an high aspiring spirit, ambitious to
s: The building of Babylon employs architects, artists, necessary materials, and two million men drawn from across the empire. The works include the city wall, bridge, embankments, palaces, a vaulted passage beneath the river, and a temple to Jupiter called Belus; the construction is presented as grand and costly, though much of it later falls into decay.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Semiramis is described as undertaking extensive works in Babylon, Media, and throughout Asia before invading India. She prepared a huge army, transportable boats, and mock elephants for the Indian campaign, but Stabrobates and the Indian army defeated her forces after battles on and beyond the Indus. Semiramis escaped across a bridge of boats and returned to Bactria with less than a third of her army. Later, after an assault arranged by her son, she surrendered the crown and disappeared, with some accounts saying she was transformed into a dove.

l: Semiramis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Semiramis built or commissioned remarkable works in Babylon, Media, and throughout Asia, including gardens, roads, palaces, canals, and monuments. She invaded India with a vast army, was wounded and defeated by Stabrobates, and escaped across the Indus. Later, after an assault arranged by her son, she surrendered the crown and disappeared.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Babylon contained a great obelisk attributed to Semiramis, along with remarkable sources of brimstone and a dangerous sulphurous spring. A nearby morass was said to seize and kill those unfamiliar with it.

l: Ecbatana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Ecbatana lay on a low, even plain and lacked a nearby spring. Semiramis built a palace there and supplied the city with abundant water through a canal from a mere beyond Mount Orontes.

l: Media, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Semiramis marched into Media, where she made a garden near Mount Bagistan, carved her image and guards into a rock, and created another garden and pleasure houses at Chaone. She also cut a passage through Mount Zarcheum and built a palace and waterworks at Ecbatana.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Semiramis later traveled through Persia and the rest of her dominions in Asia, leveling rocks and mountains, raising artificial eminences, and founding or embellishing towns and cities. Many of these works were still called Semiramis's Works.

l: Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Semiramis returned with her army to Bactria after her affairs in Egypt and Ethiopia were settled. She used Bactria as the rendezvous for her forces and as the place from which boats were transported by land toward the Indus.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: India is described as the world's greatest nation, with fertile land, abundant rivers, repeated harvests, great wealth, precious materials, and many elephants. Semiramis invaded India despite having received no provocation.

l: Stabrobates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Stabrobates was king of India and commanded immense forces, many elephants, river-boats, and an army larger than Semiramis's. He challenged Semiramis, defeated her army, wounded her in battle, and stopped pursuing her after prodigies and the advice of soothsayers.

l: Indian campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: For the Indian campaign, Semiramis ordered provinces to provide selected young men and new arms, assembled an enormous army in Bactria, and prepared boats that could be dismantled and carried overland. The campaign began with a naval victory but ended in defeat when the Indian elephants broke the Assyrian army.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: The Indus bordered India and was crossed by both fleets and armies during Semiramis's invasion. Semiramis's forces fought on the river, captured places along it, and later crossed by a bridge of boats.

l: Indian elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: The Indian elephants were numerous, strongly built, and heavily equipped to terrify their enemies. They routed and destroyed the opposing mock elephants, trampled soldiers, tore others apart, and helped defeat the Assyrian army.

l: mock elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Semiramis had three hundred thousand black oxen slaughtered so that their skins could be stitched and stuffed to resemble elephants, with men and camels placed inside. The mock elephants initially deceived the Indian scouts and frightened the Indian horses at a distance, but they were exposed and destroyed by the real Indian elephants.

l: Assyrian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: The Assyrian army included millions of infantry, hundreds of thousands of cavalry and chariots, camel-mounted soldiers, boats, and mock elephants. It initially advanced successfully but fled when the Indian elephants attacked, suffering severe losses while retreating across the bridge of boats.

l: Indian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: The Indian army was larger than Semiramis's and included many well-armored elephants, cavalry, chariots, infantry, and river-boats. After being deceived by the mock elephants, it recovered, attacked the Assyrian army, and forced it to retreat.

l: bridge of boats, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: Semiramis constructed a broad bridge of boats over the Indus and crossed it with most of her forces, leaving sixty thousand soldiers to guard it. During the retreat she ordered its cords and tenons cut, causing many Indians on the boats to drown and securing her escape.

l: Battle of the Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: The fighting at the Indus began with a naval battle in which Semiramis sank a thousand Indian vessels and took many prisoners. After her forces crossed the river, the Indian elephants defeated the Assyrian army, and Stabrobates wounded Semiramis before she fled.

l: Semiramis's disappearance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Semiramis likewise caused a great stone to be cut out of the
s: After an assault by a eunuch arranged through her son, Semiramis remembered the oracle that she would disappear when her son plotted against her. She surrendered the crown, ordered her subjects to obey him, and vanished; some accounts say she was transformed into a dove.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: After Semiramis's death, Ninyas succeeded her, and the Assyrian kings thereafter lived in seclusion and luxury until the reign of Sardanapalus. Sardanapalus's slothful and corrupt life provoked Arbaces the Mede and Belesis to organize a revolt with the Medes, Persians, Babylonians, and an Arabian king. After several defeats, the rebels gained strength when the Bactrian army joined them, defeated Sardanapalus's forces, and besieged Nineveh. When the Euphrates destroyed part of Nineveh's wall, Sardanapalus burned himself with his treasure, eunuchs, and concubines, and Arbaces became king as the Assyrian empire was overthrown.

l: Ninyas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: Ninyas, the son of Ninus and Semiramis, succeeded Semiramis and reigned peaceably. Unlike his mother, he avoided valour and martial affairs, remaining shut in his palace among his concubines and eunuchs and maintaining his rule through annually changing provincial armies and governors.

l: Sardanapalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: Sardanapalus was the thirtieth king from Ninus and the last king of the Assyrians. He exceeded his predecessors in sloth and luxury, lived in women's attire among his concubines, and practiced extreme sensuality. After Arbaces's revolt defeated his forces and besieged Nineveh, Sardanapalus burned himself, his treasure, eunuchs, and concubines in a palace fire rather than fall into enemy hands.

l: Arbaces the Mede, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: Arbaces the Mede was a valiant and prudent general who was persuaded by Belesis to attempt the overthrow of the Assyrian empire. He organized the Medes, Persians, Babylonians, and an Arabian king against Sardanapalus, suffered several defeats and was wounded, but later defeated the Assyrian forces and was proclaimed king after Nineveh fell.

l: Belesis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: Belesis was a Babylonian priest of the Chaldeans, reputed to practice astrology and divination. He persuaded Arbaces to revolt, encouraged the conspirators after their defeats by predicting success, and received the government of Babylon from Arbaces despite having secretly carried away much of Sardanapalus's gold and silver. Arbaces ultimately pardoned him, allowed him to retain Babylon, and gave him the treasure.

l: Assyrian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: The Assyrian empire continued through thirty generations from Ninus and, according to the accounts cited in the unit, for more than thirteen hundred and sixty or fourteen hundred years. It was weakened by Sardanapalus's rule and was ultimately overthrown by the Medes.

l: Assyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: The Assyrians served under Sardanapalus's command against the revolting Medes, Persians, Babylonians, and their allies. Their forces won several early battles, but were later defeated, with many killed in the fighting near Nineveh and the Euphrates.

l: Medes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: The Medes provided the annually summoned forces commanded by Arbaces. They joined the revolt against Sardanapalus, invaded the Assyrian empire with the Persians and other allies, and ultimately overthrew the Assyrian empire.

l: Nineveh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: Nineveh was the seat of Sardanapalus and was defended by strong walls and plentiful supplies. The confederates besieged it for three years until the Euphrates tore down part of its wall; they then entered the city, dispersed its inhabitants into villages, restored their estates, and razed Nineveh to the ground.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: The governor of Babylon, Belesis, joined Arbaces's conspiracy and persuaded the Babylonians to revolt. After the victory, Arbaces granted Belesis the government of Babylon without tribute, and Belesis carried Sardanapalus's ashes and much of the royal treasure there.

l: Euphrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: During the third year of the siege of Nineveh, the Euphrates overflowed after continual rains and tore down twenty furlongs of the city's wall. Its destruction of the wall fulfilled the prophecy that the river would become Nineveh's enemy.

l: revolt against Sardanapalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: The revolt was organized by Arbaces and Belesis with the Medes, Persians, Babylonians, and an Arabian king, and involved four hundred thousand soldiers from four provinces. After three initial defeats, the rebels were joined by the Bactrian army, defeated Sardanapalus's forces, and besieged Nineveh.

l: siege of Nineveh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: The siege of Nineveh lasted two years without decisive success because of the city's strong walls and the limited siege technology of the age. In the third year, the overflowing Euphrates breached twenty furlongs of wall, allowing the besiegers to enter after Sardanapalus's death.

l: overthrow of the Assyrian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IL
s: The Assyrian empire was overthrown after Arbaces's confederates defeated its forces and captured Nineveh. Arbaces was proclaimed king, appointed governors over the provinces, and transferred the remaining royal treasure to Ecbatana.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The unit describes the Chaldeans, whom the Babylonians regard as their most ancient people, and their philosophy, astrology, divination, and ideas about the heavens. It explains the Chaldeans' account of the planets, zodiac, stars, eclipses, and the structure of the world. It compares Herodotus's and Ctesias's accounts of the Medes and their empire after the fall of the Assyrian empire, including conflicts with the Cadusians and other peoples. It concludes by stating that Cyrus conquered Astyages and transferred the empire from the Medes to the Persians before turning to India.

l: Chaldeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Chaldeans are described as the most ancient Babylonians and as holding in Babylonia a position comparable to that of the Egyptian priests in Egypt. They devote themselves to divine offices, philosophy, astrology, divination, sacrifices, purifications, enchantments, the interpretation of birds, dreams, prodigies, and sacrificial entrails. They preserve their learning by hereditary tradition and claim to have observed the stars for 470,000 years when Alexander was in Asia.

l: Babylonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Babylonians call the Chaldeans their most ancient people and assign them a distinguished religious and civic position.

l: philosophy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Chaldeans hold that the world is eternal, without a definite beginning or end, and that divine providence orders and sustains it. Their philosophical learning is transmitted from fathers to sons, while the text contrasts this continuity with the competing sects and changing opinions of the Greeks.

l: astrology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Chaldeans are said to excel all others in astrology and to study the motions and influences of the stars. They use the rising, setting, and colors of stars to foretell events affecting the weather, nations, kings, and private persons.

l: planets, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Chaldeans identify five planets, which they call Interpreters: Saturn, Sol, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter is also listed among them, though the text's enumeration is inconsistent. They say that the planets move through the twelve signs of the zodiac and influence human nativities and future events.

l: Assyrian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Assyrian empire is said to have been overthrown and its rule transferred to the Medes. Herodotus is reported to have said that the Assyrians had held the empire of Asia for 500 years before their defeat by the Medes.

l: Medes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Medes conquered the Assyrians and later ruled an empire that was enlarged by successive kings. Their history is presented through differing accounts by Herodotus and Ctesias, ending with the conquest of Astyages by Cyrus.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: After the overthrow of the Assyrian empire, Ctesias says that all Asia came under the power of the Medes. The Medes retained this dominion until Cyrus conquered Astyages and transferred the empire to the Persians.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Cyrus conquered Astyages, whom the Greeks called Astyages, and thereby caused the empire to pass from the Medes to the Persians.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Persians inherited the empire after Cyrus conquered Astyages and the Medes. Ctesias is said to have used Persian public records in composing his history of earlier events.

l: Cadusians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Cadusians were persuaded by Parsodes, a Persian who had fled the Medes, to revolt and defend their liberties. They defeated a large Median army under Arsseus's successor, made Parsodes their king, and remained enemies of the Medes until Cyrus transferred the empire to the Persians.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The unit ends by announcing that the account will pass from the Assyrians and Medes to India. It does not yet provide the promised description of India.

s: The Medes' empire is described through conflicting accounts. According to Ctesias, it began under Arbaces after the overthrow of Sardanapalus, passed through a succession of kings, and ended when Cyrus conquered Astyages and transferred the empire to the Persians.

s: India is described as a quadrangular country bounded by the ocean, the mountain Hemodus, Scythia, and the river Indus. It is said to be exceptionally large, fertile, rich in metals, supplied with many rivers, and inhabited by many nations.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: The Indus is described as a very large river that runs swiftly from the north into the ocean and divides India from the rest of Asia. It receives several navigable rivers, including Hipanis, Hydaspes, and Arcesinea.

l: Ganges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: The Ganges is described as a river thirty furlongs wide that runs from north to south and empties into the ocean. Many rivers meet it, and it passes by the Gandarides, where many enormous elephants are bred.

l: Gandarides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: The Gandarides lie east of the Ganges and are said to breed multitudes of exceptionally large elephants. No foreign king had conquered them, and Alexander abandoned his planned attack after learning that they had four thousand elephants equipped for war.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Alexander is said to have conquered all of Asia and subdued the Indians behind him. He stopped his advance at the Ganges when he learned that the Gandarides possessed four thousand elephants prepared for war.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Bacchus is said by inhabitants of the mountainous parts of India to have conquered India, introduced agriculture, fruit planting, wine, cities, laws, and divine worship, and ruled for fifty-two years. He was later honored as a god, and his sons and descendants ruled after him.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: The Indians say that Hercules was born among them and surpassed other men in strength and courage. He divided India among his sons and daughter, built many cities including Palibothra, and was honored as a god after his death.

l: India's inhabitants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: India’s inhabitants are described as numerous, skilled, healthy, long-lived, and divided into seven ranks. They are said to have developed their arts gradually and to have laws regulating occupations, marriage, government, agriculture, and justice.

l: Indian philosophers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Indian philosophers are the least numerous but most esteemed social rank and are free from public offices. They perform sacrifices and funerals, advise the people through predictions about natural events, and lose the right to speak publicly if their predictions prove wrong.

l: Indian husbandmen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Indian husbandmen cultivate the land and are protected from harm even during war because they are regarded as serving the common good. They live in the fields with their families, pay tribute from their produce, and do not privately own the land.

l: Indian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Indian kings are described as owning all the land and receiving tribute, including a fourth part of agricultural produce. They maintain the soldiers, war-horses, and elephants from the treasury, and select counselors, governors, judges, and generals from the senators.

l: Indian elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Indian elephants are described as larger, stronger, and more courageous than those elsewhere, including those in Africa. They are captured, trained for war, and maintained by the king; they carry young for sixteen to eighteen months and usually bear one calf.

l: Indian rivers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Indian rivers descend from the northern mountains, water the plains, and enrich the country with gardens and fruit. The philosophers and naturalists explain their abundance by saying that rain flows down from the higher neighboring countries.

l: Indian agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Indian agriculture produces two crops each year, including wheat, rice, millet, sesamus, pulse, and a crop called Bosphorus. Rivers, summer rains, naturally growing fruits, and edible marsh roots provide additional food.

l: famine in India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: The text says that India never experiences famine or a shortage of provisions because the land yields two abundant harvests and also supplies naturally growing fruits and marsh roots. Laws protecting husbandmen from wartime devastation are said to help prevent famine.

l: Indian social ranks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: The people of India are divided into seven ranks: philosophers, husbandmen, herdsmen and shepherds, mechanics, the militia, ephori, and senators. Marriage and occupations are generally restricted to the rank into which a person was born.

l: Indian laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Indian laws include the protection of husbandmen during war, the division of society into ranks, restrictions on marriage and occupations, and provisions for strangers. One reported principle states that no one should be a servant and that all free people should receive equal respect.

l: Bacchus's conquest of India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: Bacchus is said to have entered India from the west with a large army when its inhabitants lived scattered and its cities were unable to resist him. After a plague weakened his soldiers, he moved them to the mountains, recovered them there, and later conquered and organized the country.

l: Alexander's invasion of India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, India is of a quadrangular form, one side lying towards the east^
s: During Alexander’s invasion of India, he conquered the Indians behind him and advanced as far as the Ganges. He did not attack the Gandarides after learning of their four thousand war elephants.

l: Scythians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Scythians began as a small and despised people near the river Araxes. Through valor they expanded their dominion across mountainous and plain regions, and their descendants conquered territories beyond the Tanais, as far as Egypt, the eastern ocean, the Caspian Sea, and the lake Maeotis. Their royal line eventually failed, and their nation was greatly weakened by the Sauromatians.

l: Scythian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Scythian empire grew from a small tract of ground into a vast dominion through warfare and conquest. It eventually extended toward the eastern ocean, the Caspian Sea, the lake Maeotis, the river Nile, and territories beyond the Tanais.

l: Sauromatians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Sauromatians were colonists taken from Media by Scythian kings and settled near the river Tanais. They later increased in number and power, devastated much of Scythia, and rooted out the peoples they conquered, bringing ruin to the whole Scythian nation.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Cyrus, king of Persia, led a mighty army into Scythia. The queen of Scythia defeated his army, captured him in battle, and afterward crucified him.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Persians invaded Scythia under Cyrus, but their army was routed by the queen of Scythia.

l: Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Amazons were a nation governed by women who managed martial affairs and were trained for war. They conquered neighboring peoples and large parts of Europe and Asia, but after Hercules defeated them and later wars weakened them, their nation gradually became extinct.

l: Thermodon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The river Thermodon was the setting of a powerful nation governed by female queens. The city of Themiscyra was built at its mouth.

l: Amazon queen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Amazon queens governed their nation and led its military expeditions. One especially renowned queen trained an army of women, subdued neighboring peoples, established laws assigning martial duties to women, and founded Themiscyra.

l: Themiscyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Themiscyra was a large city built by an Amazon queen at the mouth of the river Thermodon. It was beautified with a stately palace.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Amazons conquered a great part of Asia and extended their power as far as Syria.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Hercules, the son of Jupiter and Alcmena, was ordered by Eurystheus to fight Hippolyte and take her belt. He defeated the Amazons in battle and captured Hippolyte and her belt.

l: Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Hippolyte was an Amazon queen whom Hercules was ordered to fight. Hercules captured her and took her belt.

l: Trojan War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Trojan War began a few years after Hercules's time. During the war, Penthesilea brought aid to the Trojans after the death of Hector.

l: Penthesilea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Penthesilea was the queen of the Amazons who remained after Hercules's time and was said to be a daughter of Mars. She aided the Trojans, killed many Greeks, and was eventually slain by Achilles.

l: Hyperboreans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Hyperboreans inhabited an island in the ocean beyond Gaul and the north wind. They were described as prosperous people with a temperate climate, a special friendship for the Greeks, and a religious devotion to Apollo.

l: Hyperborean island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Hyperborean island lay in the ocean opposite Gaul and was said to be as large as Sicily. It had rich soil, a temperate climate, a sacred grove, a round temple to Apollo, and a city consecrated to that god.

l: Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Apollo was worshipped above all other gods by the Hyperboreans because Latona was said to have been born on their island. He was believed to visit the island once in nineteen years, when he played the harp, sang, and danced from the vernal equinox until the rising of the Pleiades.

l: Apollo's temple, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Apollo's temple on the Hyperborean island was described as a renowned, round structure beautified with many rich gifts. Sacred hymns praising Apollo were sung there by harpers.

l: Scythian conquest and expansion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Scythians expanded from the area near the Araxes across the mountains to Caucasus, the plains toward the ocean and lake Maeotis, and the plain to the Tanais. Their descendants later conquered territories beyond the Tanais and extended their power toward Egypt, the eastern ocean, the Caspian Sea, and lake Maeotis.

l: Amazon wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Amazons conquered neighboring nations and extended their wars into Europe and Asia. Their wars eventually weakened them after Hercules defeated them, and surrounding peoples continued attacking them until their nation disappeared.

l: Hercules's expedition against the Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: Hercules undertook an expedition against the Amazons at the command of Eurystheus. He routed them in battle and took Hippolyte and her belt, after which the Amazons became vulnerable to attacks from neighboring peoples.

l: Amazons' extinction, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: After Hercules's victory, the Amazons were repeatedly attacked and greatly reduced. Following Penthesilea's death, their nation grew weaker until it was wholly extinct, and later ages regarded their earlier exploits as fictions and fables.

l: Hyperborean religion and Apollo worship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Scytliians anti^ntly enjoyed but a small tract of ground
s: The Hyperboreans worshipped Apollo above all other gods and honored him with songs, sacrifices, and sacred ceremonies. Their city contained harpers who sang hymns about his glorious acts, and their island had a sacred grove and temple dedicated to him.

s: This unit describes Arabia, including Arabia the Desert and Arabia the Happy, their peoples, resources, animals, plants, and trade. The Nabatheans inhabit a dry and partly waterless region, preserve their liberty through secret wells and fortified places, and resist foreign conquest. Arabia the Happy is praised for its aromatic plants, precious materials, fertile lands, abundant cattle, unusual beasts, and valuable commerce. The sun is said to produce or influence the colors, forms, fertility, smells, and properties of living creatures, stones, plants, and the earth.

l: Arabia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Arabia is described as lying between Syria and Egypt and as being divided into several nations. It contains desert and fertile regions, produces aromatic plants, balsam, gold, precious stones, cattle, unusual beasts, and valuable fruits, and supports farmers, shepherds, merchants, and traders.

l: Arabia the Desert, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Arabia the Desert is a barren and dry region with little fruit, especially in the country inhabited by the Nabatheans. It contains hidden wells, a fortified rock, and a large brimstone-producing mere, while its watered areas support palm-trees and balsam.

l: Arabia the Happy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Arabia the Happy is the fertile southern part of Arabia, known for its abundance of aromatic plants, gums, myrrh, frankincense, valuable stone, gold, cattle, fruits, and strange animals. Its rivers and summer rains create ponds and lakes, allowing some areas to produce two harvests.

l: Nabatheans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Nabatheans inhabit a partly desert and waterless region and live by raiding and robbery because little of their land bears fruit. They use secret wells for refuge, remain free from foreign rulers, and have resisted the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, and Macedonians.

l: the sun, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The sun is said to create and influence the forms, colors, fertility, smells, tastes, size, and properties of things throughout the southern regions. Its heat is described as hardening stones, producing precious stones, nourishing the earth and water, and causing the variety of creatures and plants.
